summary: Source decomposition from three primary sources read directly: Rubin's Euler Systems author draft (Ch. I Sections 2, 3.1, 5, 7 and all of Appendix B), Nekovar's Selmer complexes (Asterisque 310) INTRODUCTION Sections 0.8-0.13 only, and Rodrigues Jacinto-Williams Sec. 13.5 read in full. Four points are recorded. (1) THE KUMMER IDENTIFICATION IS A COMPLETION: Rubin Example 2.1 writes H^1(K,Z_p(1)) = inverse limit of K^x/(K^x)^{p^n} = K^x COMPLETED-tensor Z_p, and the inverse-limit step is Prop. B.2.3, which needs finiteness of H^0(K, mu_{p^n}); this is exactly the stage's warning against replacing the completion by an algebraic tensor product. (2) THE LONG EXACT SEQUENCE IN CONTINUOUS COHOMOLOGY IS CONDITIONAL on the existence of a continuous set-theoretic section, and Rubin states the three coefficient situations in which he uses it. Relatedly, Nekovar states that no satisfactory general Hochschild-Serre formalism for continuous cohomology exists, and defines his unramified local conditions by explicit formulas instead. (3) THE SELMER COMPLEX IS A MAPPING FIBRE AND ITS COHOMOLOGY DOES NOT INJECT into global cohomology; Nekovar's worked ordinary-elliptic-curve comparison exhibits the extra term H^0(G_p,T^-), which detects a trivial zero, and a finite error group C whose order at each v is the local Tamagawa factor. Nekovar also restricts to Greenberg's local conditions because 'the general case would require a heavy dose of crystalline machinery, which is not yet available'. (4) THE IWASAWA IDENTIFICATION CARRIES A TWIST AND AN INVOLUTION: RGamma_Iw = RGamma_cont(G_{K,S}, (T tensor R(Gamma))<-1>), the degeneration of the Ext spectral sequences holds only modulo pseudo-null modules, and the Iwasawa Selmer-complex duality needs the hypothesis that no prime of Sigma_f splits completely in K_infinity/K. For L4, Greenberg's Conjecture 13.21 is recorded with its ordinarity hypothesis, its separate corank and characteristic-ideal assertions, the conditionality of the latter on r_V = r_{V-dual} = 0, and RJW's Remark 13.23 showing the case n = 0 is not covered. All five stages are partial. Only the introduction of Nekovar was read; Rubin Ch. I Sections 3.2-4 and RJW Sec. 10.5 remain unread; Poitou-Tate, local Tate duality, Greenberg's and Coates-Perrin-Riou's papers, Coates-Sujatha and a determinant-of-a-complex source are all absent from the supplied library.

nodes.title: Tate's continuous cochain cohomology and the exactness hypothesis
nodes.statement: For G profinite and T a topological G-module, set C^i(G,T) = Maps(G^i, T) (continuous maps, compact-open topology) with the usual coboundaries, and H^i(G,T) = ker d^i / im d^{i-1}. A short exact sequence 0 -> T' -> T -> T'' -> 0 gives a short exact sequence of cochain complexes, and hence a long exact cohomology sequence, PROVIDED there is a continuous set-theoretic section T'' -> T. Such a section exists when T'' is topologically discrete (equivalently when T' is open in T), and when T is a finitely generated Z_p-module or a finite-dimensional Q_p-vector space with its usual topology.
hypotheses: The cochains are continuous MAPS, not necessarily homomorphisms; this is Tate's definition and differs from the naive derived-functor definition

The long exact sequence is NOT automatic: it requires a continuous set-theoretic section of T -> T''. Rubin states explicitly that the three listed situations are the only ones in which he uses these groups
No claim is made for arbitrary topological G-modules
proofSteps: Define C^i(G,T) with the compact-open topology and the usual coboundary formulas.
Given a continuous section of T -> T'', the sequence of cochain groups is exact in each degree, because a continuous cochain into T'' lifts by composing with the section.
Take the long exact sequence of the resulting short exact sequence of complexes.
Verify the section exists in the three listed cases.
acceptance: Exhibit a short exact sequence of topological G-modules with no continuous section and check the long exact sequence fails
Check the definition agrees with the usual profinite group cohomology for discrete torsion T
Check H^1(K, Q_p/Z_p) = Hom(G_K, Q_p/Z_p) and H^1(K, Z_p) = Hom(G_K, Z_p)

sources.locator: Appendix B, Definition 2.1 and Remark 2.2, printed pp. 151-152
sources.excerpt: If 0 -> T' -> T -> T'' -> 0 is an exact sequence and if there is a continuous section (again a set map, not necessarily a homomorphism) from T'' -> T, then 0 -> C^i(G,T') -> C^i(G,T) -> C^i(G,T'') -> 0 is exact for every i and there is a long exact sequence
sources.match: The hypothesis that makes the long exact sequence available; this is the 'correct cohomological hypotheses and topologies' the stage insists on.

sources.excerpt: when T is a finitely generated Z_p-module, or a finite-dimensional Q_p-vector space, with the usual topology, there is a continuous section. These are the only situations in which we will use these cohomology groups.
sources.match: Delimits exactly the coefficient categories in which the source's statements are valid.

nodes.title: Comparison of continuous cohomology with inverse limits and with rationalization
nodes.statement: (i) If T = inverse limit of T_n with each T_n finite discrete and i > 0, and if H^{i-1}(G,T_n) is finite for every n, then H^i(G,T) = inverse limit of H^i(G,T_n). (ii) If T is a finitely generated Z_p-module then H^i(G,T) has no divisible elements and H^i(G,T) tensor Q_p -> H^i(G, T tensor Q_p) is an isomorphism. (iii) Inflation-restriction is exact in low degrees, and under the finiteness hypothesis that H^1 and H^2 of G and H^1 of H are finite on all modules of finite p-power order, the five-term Hochschild-Serre sequence extends to 0 -> H^1(G/H, T^H) -> H^1(G,T) -> H^1(H,T)^{G/H} -> H^2(G/H, T^H) -> H^2(G,T) for T discrete, or finitely generated over Z_p, or a finite-dimensional Q_p-vector space.
hypotheses: (i) requires the finiteness of H^{i-1}(G,T_n) for EVERY n; this is the exactness-of-inverse-limits input and is exactly the hypothesis the stage asks to record per tower
(iii) requires the finiteness hypothesis on H^1 and H^2 of G and H^1 of H; Rubin's Remark 2.6 notes this holds whenever the pro-p part of G is topologically finitely generated
The extended Hochschild-Serre sequence is NOT proved in general: it is proved for T/p^n T (discrete) and then obtained by an inverse limit using (i), which is where the finiteness is used again
proofSteps: (iii) For T discrete the sequence is standard. For T finitely generated over Z_p, apply the discrete case to T/p^n T, note all terms are finite by hypothesis, and pass to the inverse limit using (i).
For T a finite-dimensional Q_p-vector space, choose a G-stable Z_p-lattice T_0, run the previous case, tensor with Q_p and use (ii).
Proposition 1.1(i): an inverse system of short exact sequences with COMPACT left terms has exact inverse limit; this is the exactness input for towers.
acceptance: Check the finiteness hypothesis for G = Gal(K_Sigma/K) with K a number field and Sigma finite (Rubin Proposition 2.7(i))
Exhibit a tower where the finiteness fails and the inverse limit comparison breaks
Check H^1(G, T) = T/(gamma-1)T for G isomorphic to Zhat with topological generator gamma (Lemma 2.8)

sources.excerpt: Suppose i > 0 and T = inverse limit of T_n where each T_n is a finite (discrete) G-module. If H^{i-1}(G,T_n) is finite for every n then H^i(G,T) = inverse limit of H^i(G,T_n).
sources.match: The comparison the stage calls the derived-limit/lim^1 input, in the form actually used, with its finiteness hypothesis.

sources.excerpt: Then for every n >= 0, T/p^n T is discrete so there is a Hochschild-Serre exact sequence for T/p^n T. Our hypotheses ensure that all the terms in this sequence are finite, and so taking the inverse limit over n and applying Proposition 2.3 gives the exact sequence of (ii) for T.
sources.match: Shows that the 'full Hochschild-Serre' for non-discrete coefficients is obtained by a limit under finiteness, not by a general formalism.

sources.excerpt: Unfortunately, there does not seem to be a satisfactory general formalism of the Hochschild-Serre spectral sequence for continuous cohomology. As a result, we define C_ur by explicit formulas.

nodes.title: H^1(K, Z_p(1)) is the p-adic completion of K^x, not an algebraic tensor product
nodes.statement: For K a field of characteristic not p, Kummer theory gives H^1(K, mu_{p^n}) = K^x/(K^x)^{p^n} and hence H^1(K, mu_{p^infinity}) = K^x tensor Q_p/Z_p; passing to the inverse limit using the continuous-cohomology comparison gives H^1(K, Z_p(1)) = inverse limit over n of H^1(K, mu_{p^n}) = inverse limit over n of K^x/(K^x)^{p^n}, which is the COMPLETED tensor product K^x completed-tensor Z_p, not the algebraic tensor product K^x tensor Z_p.
hypotheses: char K is not p, so Kummer theory applies and mu_{p^n} has the right size
The inverse limit step is Rubin Proposition B.2.3 with i = 1, which needs H^0(K, mu_{p^n}) finite for every n; that holds since mu_{p^n}(K) is finite

K^x is in general NOT finitely generated (this is the point of the stage's warning); the algebraic tensor product K^x tensor Z_p is therefore not the completion, and Rubin's notation is explicitly the completed tensor product
For units, S-units and local multiplicative groups the two agree only when the group involved is finitely generated, which must be proved separately in each case
proofSteps: Kummer theory gives the exact sequence and hence H^1(K, mu_{p^n}) = K^x/(K^x)^{p^n}.
For the direct limit, H^1(K, mu_{p^infinity}) = K^x tensor Q_p/Z_p.
For the inverse limit, apply Proposition B.2.3 with T = Z_p(1) = inverse limit of mu_{p^n} and i = 1; the hypothesis is finiteness of H^0(K, mu_{p^n}).
Identify the resulting inverse limit with the p-adic completion of K^x.
acceptance: For K a number field, check that the natural map from the algebraic tensor product O_{K,S}^x tensor Z_p to H^1 is an isomorphism (S-units ARE finitely generated), and that the same statement for K^x is false
For K a p-adic field, check the completion against the structure of K^x
Check tower compatibility under the norm/corestriction maps

sources.locator: Ch. I Sec. 2, Example 2.1, printed p. 3
sources.excerpt: and by Kummer theory and Proposition B.2.3, respectively H^1(K, mu_{p^infinity}) = K^x tensor (Q_p/Z_p), H^1(K, Z_p(1)) = inverse limit of H^1(K, mu_{p^n}) = inverse limit of K^x/(K^x)^{p^n} = K^x completed-tensor Z_p, where completed-tensor denotes the (p-adically) completed tensor product.
sources.match: Exactly the identification the stage requires, with the source itself writing the COMPLETED tensor product, which is the point the stage warns about.

nodes.title: Poitou-Tate duality in the form that identifies the annihilator of a local condition
nodes.statement: Let K be a number field, T a p-adic representation of G_K ramified at finitely many primes, and for v dividing p fix H^1_f(K_v,V) and H^1_f(K_v,V^*) that are ORTHOGONAL COMPLEMENTS under the local Tate pairing. For M nonzero in O and finite sets Sigma_0 contained in Sigma of places: (i) there are exact sequences 0 -> S^{Sigma_0}(K,W_M) -> S^Sigma(K,W_M) -> sum over v in Sigma - Sigma_0 of H^1_s(K_v,W_M) and 0 -> S_Sigma(K,W_M^*) -> S_{Sigma_0}(K,W_M^*) -> sum of H^1_f(K_v,W_M^*); (ii) the images of these two localization maps are EXACT ORTHOGONAL COMPLEMENTS under the sum of the local pairings; (iii) S_{Sigma_0}(K,W_M^*)/S_Sigma(K,W_M^*) is isomorphic to Hom_O(coker(loc^s_{Sigma,Sigma_0}), O/MO).
hypotheses: The orthogonality of H^1_f(K_v,V) and H^1_f(K_v,V^*) at v dividing p is a HYPOTHESIS, not automatic. Rubin's Remark 7.1 records that it holds when V is potentially semistable at v, citing Bloch-Kato and Fontaine-Perrin-Riou
At v not dividing p the relevant statement is that H^1_ur(K_v, W_M) and H^1_ur(K_v, W_M^*) are orthogonal complements; this is where the unramified condition's annihilator is computed
The proof reduces to the case where Sigma contains all infinite places, all primes above p and all primes of ramification, so that S^Sigma(K, W_M) = H^1(K_Sigma/K, W_M) by Lemma 5.3
The global input is the Poitou-Tate exact sequence, quoted from Milne, Arithmetic Duality Theorems Thm. I.4.10, or Tate; that sequence is NOT proved in Rubin
proofSteps: (i) is immediate from the definitions of the Selmer groups.
(ii) Use the nondegenerate local pairing H^1_s(K_v, W_M) x H^1_f(K_v, W_M^*) -> O/MO from Theorem 4.1 and Proposition 4.3(ii).
Reduce to Sigma large, so that both Selmer groups are H^1(K_Sigma/K, -) by Lemma 5.3.
Insert the segment S^Sigma(K,W_M) -> sum over v in Sigma of H^1(K_v, W_M) -> S^Sigma(K, W_M^*)^dual of the Poitou-Tate sequence.
(iii) follows from (ii) by dualizing the cokernel.
acceptance: Compute the annihilator of the unramified condition at a prime of good reduction and check it is the unramified condition on the dual
Check the potential-semistability hypothesis is needed at v dividing p by exhibiting a non-orthogonal pair otherwise
Check (iii) with Sigma_0 empty, recovering the standard bound used by Euler systems

sources.locator: Ch. I Sec. 7, Theorem 7.3, printed pp. 17-18
sources.excerpt: (ii) The images loc^s_{Sigma,Sigma_0}(S^Sigma(K,W_M)) and loc^f_{Sigma,Sigma_0}(S_{Sigma_0}(K,W_M^*)) are orthogonal complements of each other with respect to the pairing sum over v in Sigma - Sigma_0 of < , >_v.

nodes.title: The relaxed and strict Selmer groups attached to a finite set Sigma
nodes.statement: Let K be a number field, T a p-adic representation of G_K unramified outside a finite set, and for each place v a choice of H^1_f(K_v, -) with H^1_s(K_v, -) = H^1(K_v,-)/H^1_f(K_v,-). For a finite set Sigma of places define S^Sigma(K,W) = ker(H^1(K,W) -> sum over v not in Sigma of H^1_s(K_v,W)) (relaxed at Sigma) and S_Sigma(K,W) = ker(S^Sigma(K,W) -> sum over v in Sigma of H^1(K_v,W)) (strict at Sigma); with Sigma empty both equal S(K,W). The same definitions are made for T and for W_M. If Sigma contains all primes above p then S^Sigma and S_Sigma do not depend on the choice of H^1_f at p. If Sigma contains all infinite places, all primes above p and all primes of ramification, then S^Sigma(K,A) = H^1(K_Sigma/K, A) for A = T, W or W_M.
hypotheses: The sum over v not in Sigma is well defined because a class restricts to zero in all but finitely many H^1_s(K_v,W); this uses that T is ramified at only finitely many primes
Lemma 5.3 needs H^1_f(K_v,A) = H^1_ur(K_v,A) for v outside Sigma, which is Rubin's Lemmas 3.5(iv) and 3.8(ii) and requires v not dividing p
Lemma 5.4 (the imprimitive surjection) holds for the RELAXED groups S^Sigma; Remark 5.5 records that it may FAIL for the strict groups S_Sigma
The passage between T, V and W is governed by Lemma 2.2(iii): the kernel of H^1(K,T) -> H^1(K,W) is M H^1(K,T) + H^1(K,T)_tors, so saturation statements are separate lemmas
proofSteps: Define H^1_s as the quotient by the chosen local condition and form the two kernels.
Lemma 5.3: for v outside Sigma the condition is the unramified one, so S^Sigma(K,A) = ker(H^1(K,A) -> product of Hom(I_v,A)) = ker(H^1(K,A) -> H^1(K_Sigma,A)) = H^1(K_Sigma/K,A).
Lemma 5.4: by Lemma 2.2(i) the image of H^1(K,W_M) in H^1(K,W) is H^1(K,W)_M, and the preimage of S^Sigma(K,W)_M is S^Sigma(K,W_M); hence the surjection.
Lemma 2.2(iii) gives the kernel of the change-of-coefficients map and hence the lattice-change formulas.
acceptance: Recover the classical p-power Selmer group of an abelian variety as S(K, A[p^infinity]) (Rubin Proposition 6.7)
Check that S^Sigma(K,W_M) -> S^Sigma(K,W)_M is surjective but that the analogous map for S_Sigma need not be
Check independence of the choice at p when Sigma contains all primes above p

sources.locator: Ch. I Sec. 5, Definition 5.1, printed pp. 11-12
sources.excerpt: S^Sigma(K,W) consists of all classes c in H^1(K,W) satisfying the local conditions: c_v in H^1_f(K_v,W) if v not in Sigma, no restriction for v in Sigma, and S_Sigma(K,W) has the additional restrictions c_v = 0 if v in Sigma.
sources.match: The relaxed and strict conditions the stage asks to define separately, stated on the actual cohomology groups.

sources.locator: Ch. I Sec. 5, Lemma 5.3 with proof, printed p. 12
sources.excerpt: Suppose Sigma contains all infinite places, all primes above p, and all primes of K where T is ramified. If A = T, W, or W_M with M in O, then S^Sigma(K,A) = H^1(K_Sigma/K,A).
sources.match: The comparison with the ramification-restricted cohomology, with the exact hypothesis on Sigma.

sources.locator: Ch. I Sec. 5, Lemma 5.4 and Remark 5.5, printed p. 12

nodes.title: The Selmer complex, its exact triangle, and why only Greenberg conditions are treated
nodes.statement: Let X be a bounded complex of admissible R[G_{K,S}]-modules. Local conditions are a collection A(X) = (i_v^+(X) : U_v^+(X) -> C_cont(G_v, X))_{v in S_f} of morphisms of complexes of R-modules with U_v^+(X) satisfying finiteness conditions. The Selmer complex is the total complex of C_cont(G_{K,S},X) + sum over v of U_v^+(X) -> sum over v of C_cont(G_v,X); writing U_v^-(X) = Cone(i_v^+), the exact triangle RGamma_f(X) -> RGamma_cont(G_{K,S},X) -> sum over v of U_v^-(X) gives the long exact sequence (0.8.0.1). IN PARTICULAR the canonical map H^i_f(X) -> H^i_cont(G_{K,S},X) NEED NOT BE INJECTIVE. Nekovar treats only Greenberg's local conditions: for v in a subset Sigma containing all primes above p one is given a morphism X_v^+ -> X and sets U_v^+(X) = C_cont(G_v, X_v^+); for the remaining v one takes explicitly defined unramified complexes.
hypotheses: The local conditions are morphisms of COMPLEXES, not submodules of cohomology; the stage's 'submodules or maps of complexes' must be read as the latter for the Selmer complex
The Selmer complex is a mapping fibre, so its cohomology does NOT inject into global cohomology in general; the failure is measured by the U_v^- terms

Nekovar states explicitly that Greenberg's are 'the only local conditions that can be handled by elementary methods; the general case would require a heavy dose of crystalline machinery, which is not yet available'. So Bloch-Kato conditions are NOT covered by this source

The unramified conditions are defined by explicit formulas because no general Hochschild-Serre formalism for continuous cohomology is available; for X = A^0 concentrated in degree 0 the explicit complex is (X^0)^{I_v} -> (X^0)^{I_v} with the map f_v - 1, in degrees 0 and 1
Greenberg's filtration is a G_v-stable (decomposition group) subobject X_v^+ -> X, not a globally stable one
proofSteps: Form the total complex of the displayed two-term diagram of complexes; this is by definition the mapping fibre of the difference of the global localization and the local conditions.
Set U_v^-(X) = Cone(i_v^+(X)) and read off the exact triangle and the long exact sequence.
For Greenberg's conditions, take U_v^+(X) = C_cont(G_v, X_v^+) for v in Sigma and the explicit unramified complex otherwise.
Record that the canonical map to global cohomology is not injective, so that H^i_f is an 'extended' Selmer group.
acceptance: Check Nekovar's elliptic-curve computation: for E/Q ordinary at p with p not 2 there is an exact sequence 0 -> H^0(G_p, T^-) -> H^1_f(T) -> Sel(G_{Q,S},T) -> C -> 0 with C finite and H^0(G_p,T^-) nonzero exactly in the split multiplicative case
Check the explicit unramified complex computes H^1_ur in degrees 0 and 1
Check the mapping-fibre construction reproduces the classical Selmer group under the stated H^0 vanishing

sources.excerpt: Selmer groups have been traditionally defined as subgroups of elements of H^1(G_{K,S}, -) satisfying suitable local conditions in H^1(G_v, -) (for v in S). In our approach we have no choice but to impose local conditions on the level of complexes, rather than cohomology.
sources.match: States the design decision the stage's 'Construct the Selmer complex as an actual mapping fibre' demands, and the reason for it.

sources.excerpt: In particular, the canonical map H^i_f(X) -> H^i_cont(G_{K,S},X) need not be injective.
sources.match: The precise failure that distinguishes the Selmer complex from the classical Selmer group; it must not be suppressed.

sources.excerpt: In the present work we consider only Greenberg's local conditions, defined as follows (these are the only local conditions that can be handled by elementary methods; the general case would require a heavy dose of crystalline machinery, which is not yet available).
sources.match: Confirms that Bloch-Kato local conditions are outside this source's scope, matching the stage's decision to defer them to L4.

sources.excerpt: 0 -> H^0(G_p,T^-) -> H^1_f(T) -> Sel(G_{Q,S},T) -> C -> 0, in which C is a finite group ... In other words, H^1_f(T) is an 'extended Selmer group' in the sense of Mazur, Tate and Teitelbaum and the term H^0(G_p,T^-) detects the presence of a 'trivial zero' of the p-adic L-function of E.
sources.match: The worked comparison with the classical Selmer group under Greenberg conditions, including the exact error terms; this is the 'prove its cohomology gives the classical group under the stated H^0 conditions' item.

nodes.title: RGamma_Iw(K_infinity/K, T) = RGamma_cont(G_{K,S}, F_Gamma(T)) with the twist and involution made explicit
nodes.statement: Let K be a number field, S as usual, K contained in K_infinity contained in K_S Galois with Gamma = Gal(K_infinity/K) isomorphic to Z_p^r (or Z_p^r times a finite abelian A), G = G_{K,S}, and R_tilde = R(Gamma) = inverse limit of R[Gal(K_alpha/K)]. Let chi_Gamma : G -> Gamma -> R_tilde^x be the tautological character and iota the R-linear involution with iota(gamma) = gamma^{-1}. For an R[G]-module M, M<n> is M with g acting by chi_Gamma(g)^n g, and M^iota is M with gamma acting by iota(gamma). Then Shapiro's Lemma gives H^i_Iw(K_infinity/K,T) = inverse limit over alpha of H^i_cont(Gal(K_S/K_alpha),T) = H^i(RGamma_cont(G_{K,S}, F_Gamma(T))) where F_Gamma(T) = (T tensor_R R_tilde)<-1>, and dually H^i(K_S/K_infinity, A) = H^i(RGamma_cont(G_{K,S}, F_Gamma(A))) with F_Gamma(A) = Hom_{R,cont}(R_tilde, A)<-1>.
hypotheses: The twist by <-1> is part of the statement: the induced module carries the tautological character to the power -1, which is exactly the 'inverse Galois action precisely specified' the stage demands
The involution iota must be carried in all duality statements; the dual of an Iwasawa module is an R_tilde-module through iota
T and A are bounded complexes of admissible R[G]-modules of finite (resp. co-finite) type over R

Apply Shapiro's Lemma layer by layer (Nekovar Sections 8.3 and 8.4) to identify the inverse limit of the H^i over the tower with the cohomology of the induced module.

nodes.title: Poitou-Tate duality over the Iwasawa algebra and the Ext spectral sequences
nodes.statement: Applying Poitou-Tate duality over R_tilde to the duality diagram (0.12.1) for F_Gamma(T), F_Gamma(T^*), F_Gamma(A), F_Gamma(A^*) yields a duality diagram relating RGamma_Iw(K_infinity/K,T) and RGamma_{c,Iw}(K_infinity/K, T^*(1))[3], and spectral sequences of the form E_2^{i,j} = Ext^i_{R_tilde}(D(H^{-j}(K_S/K_infinity,A)), R_tilde) converging to H^{i+j}_Iw(K_infinity/K,T). Since codim supp E_2^{i,j} is at least i, the spectral sequence degenerates in the quotient category (R_tilde Mod)/(pseudo-null) into short exact sequences in which one term has no R_tilde-torsion and the other has support in codimension at least 1. In the classical case R = Z_p the spectral sequence is Jannsen's.

nodes.title: Selmer complexes over the tower and the hypothesis on completely split primes
nodes.statement: Given compatible systems of local conditions U_v^+(X) along the tower {K_alpha}, one defines Selmer complexes RGamma_{f,Iw}(K_infinity/K, X) for X = T, T^*(1) and RGamma_f(K_S/K_infinity, Y) for Y = A, A^*(1). Over each finite layer the duality diagram may carry nonzero error terms, but their limit over the tower is very often pseudo-null (or co-pseudo-null). For Greenberg's local conditions this holds under the hypothesis that NO PRIME v in Sigma_f SPLITS COMPLETELY in K_infinity/K.

The vanishing of the error terms in the limit is only 'up to pseudo-null' and only under the non-splitting hypothesis on primes in Sigma_f
Greenberg's local conditions have a built-in base change property (Nekovar 0.14.3), which is what makes the compatible system exist

Compare the finite-layer duality diagrams; the error terms Err_v are finite at each layer with order the local Tamagawa factor of T at v.
Under the non-splitting hypothesis the limits of these error terms become pseudo-null, which is what Nekovar records at Sec. 8.9.9.

nodes.title: Selmer structures, the Greenberg condition at p, and the Bloch-Kato condition
nodes.statement: Let M be a topological O_L-module with a continuous O_L-linear G_F-action unramified outside a finite set. A Selmer structure L = (L_v) for M over F is a choice of subspace L_v of H^1(F_v, M) for every finite place v, with L_v = H^1_ur(F_v,M) for almost all v, where H^1_ur(F_v,M) = ker(H^1(F_v,M) -> H^1(I_{F_v},M)). The Selmer group is H^1_L(F,M) = ker(H^1(F,M) -> sum over finite v of H^1(F_v,M)/L_v). Greenberg's condition at p assumes V is p-ORDINARY, i.e. there is a saturated finite G_Q-invariant filtration Fil^i of V on which the inertia group I_{Q_p} acts on Fil^i/Fil^{i+1} by the i-th power of the cyclotomic character; then L_{v_p}^{Gr} = ker(H^1(F_{v_p},W) -> H^1(I_{v_p},W) -> H^1(I_{v_p}, W/Fil^1 W)). The Bloch-Kato condition is L_{v_p}^{BK} = image of H^1_f(F_{v_p},V) = ker(H^1(F_{v_p},V) -> H^1(F_{v_p}, V tensor B_cris)) in H^1(F_{v_p},W).
hypotheses: RJW work over F = F_infinity^+ = Q(mu_{p^infinity})^+, NOT over the cyclotomic Z_p-extension Q_infinity/Q as Greenberg does; they flag the difference explicitly

The Greenberg condition requires V to be p-ordinary in the stated strong sense: a SATURATED, FINITE, G_Q-invariant filtration with inertia acting by powers of the cyclotomic character on the graded pieces
The Bloch-Kato condition needs B_cris, i.e. the period rings, which is why it cannot be an input to the earlier cohomology construction
The two conditions coincide in some fundamental examples but not in general; RJW refer to Kato and Perrin-Riou Sec. 2.4.7 for the relation
Only Selmer structures with unramified conditions away from p are considered in what follows
proofSteps: Definition 13.18 fixes the notion of Selmer structure and Selmer group with the almost-all-unramified requirement.
Definition 13.19(1) constructs the Greenberg condition from the ordinary filtration by composing restriction to inertia with the projection modulo Fil^1.
Definition 13.19(2) constructs the Bloch-Kato condition from H^1_f(F_{v_p},V) and pushes it into H^1(F_{v_p},W).
Remark 13.20 records that the two agree in fundamental examples without asserting a general comparison.
acceptance: Check H^1_ur is the kernel of restriction to inertia, not the kernel of restriction to the decomposition group
Check that Greenberg's filtration is stable under the decomposition group at p and need not be globally stable
Compare the two conditions for an ordinary elliptic curve

Here, the unramified cohomology groups are defined as H^1_ur(F_v,M) = ker(H^1(F_v,M) -> H^1(I_{F_v},M)), where I_{F_v} denotes the inertia group of F_v and the map is restriction.

nodes.title: Recovering X_infinity and Y_infinity from Selmer groups of Z_p(n), with the parity restrictions
nodes.statement: Let p be odd, F_infinity = Q(mu_{p^infinity}), F = F_infinity^+, T_n = Z_p(n), W_n = (Q_p/Z_p)(n). Then H^1(F,W_n) = Hom_{cts,{+-1}}(G_{F_infinity}, W_n), and for n > 0 the Greenberg Selmer group H^1_{L_Gr}(F_infinity, W_n) = Hom_cts((X_infinity)^{c = (-1)^n}, W_n), while for n <= 0 it equals Hom_cts((Y_infinity)^{c = (-1)^n}, W_n). Here X_infinity = Gal(M_infinity/F_infinity) with M_infinity the maximal abelian pro-p extension of F_infinity unramified outside p, and Y_infinity its unramified analogue. The natural surjection X_infinity -> X_infinity^+ induces an isomorphism (X_infinity)^{c=1} = X_infinity^+, and similarly for Y. Consequently for EVEN POSITIVE n, H^1_{L_Gr}(F_infinity, W_n) = Hom_cts(X_infinity^+, W_n), a twist of the Pontryagin dual of the module X_infinity^+ appearing in the Main Conjecture.
hypotheses: p ODD: the inflation-restriction identification H^1(F,W_n) = H^1(G_{F_infinity},W_n)^{+-1} uses that Gal(F_infinity/F) = {1,c} has order 2 prime to p
c acts on W_n as (-1)^n, which is what produces the parity split between even and odd n
The identification (X_infinity)^{c=1} = X_infinity^+ is quoted from Coates-Sujatha p. 6
The statement splits at n > 0 versus n <= 0: X_infinity for positive n and Y_infinity for non-positive n. This is the 'even-positive/odd-negative restriction' the stage names
proofSteps: Since G_{F_infinity} acts trivially on W_n, H^1(F_infinity,W_n) = Hom_cts(G_{F_infinity},W_n).
Inflation-restriction with Gal(F_infinity/F) = {1,c} of order 2 and p odd gives H^1(F,W_n) = Hom_{cts,{+-1}}(G_{F_infinity},W_n).
Since W_n is abelian and p-power torsion, factor through the maximal abelian pro-p quotient Gal(F_infinity^{ab,pro-p}/F_infinity).
Unramifiedness away from p makes sigma descend to X_infinity; the condition at p separates X_infinity from Y_infinity according to the sign of n.
Use c acting by (-1)^n and the Coates-Sujatha identification to reach X_infinity^+ for even positive n.

nodes.title: Greenberg's Main Conjecture and its criticality hypotheses
nodes.statement: Let T, V, W be as above with V ordinary at p, and V^dual = Hom_cts(V, Q_p(1)) the Tate dual. Let L(V,s) be the L-function of V, L_infinity(V,s) the Gamma factor (which has no zeros), and r_V the order of the pole of L_infinity(V,s) at s = 1. Coates and Perrin-Riou conjectured the existence of a p-adic L-function for V in the fraction field of Lambda(Gamma^+). Greenberg's conjecture: (i) H^1_{L_Gr}(F,W) has Lambda(Gamma^+)-corank equal to r_V; (ii) IF r_V = r_{V^dual} = 0, then the characteristic ideal of the Pontryagin dual of H^1_{L_Gr}(F,W) as a Lambda(Gamma^+)-module coincides with the ideal generated by the p-adic L-function of V.
hypotheses: V must be ORDINARY at p for the Greenberg Selmer group to be defined
Part (ii) is CONDITIONAL on r_V = r_{V^dual} = 0; the positive-rank statement is a different assertion and is not part of this conjecture
The existence of the p-adic L-function is itself the separate Coates-Perrin-Riou conjecture; Greenberg's conjecture PRESUPPOSES it and does not prove it

The case V = Q_p (n = 0) is NOT covered: RJW's Remark 13.23 shows the underlying criticality assumption fails there, since L_infinity(Q_p^dual, s) = L_infinity(Q_p, 1-s) forces r_{Q_p^dual} = 1. In Greenberg's terminology L(Q_p(n),1) = zeta(1-n) and L(Q_p(n)^dual,1) = zeta(n) are both critical only when n is even and strictly positive, or n is odd and negative
Noncommutative versions exist and are attributed to Kato and to Fukaya-Kato; they are different statements
proofSteps: State the conjecture as RJW do, with the corank assertion (i) and the conditional characteristic-ideal assertion (ii).

Example 13.22: for even positive n, the Pontryagin dual is X_infinity^+(-n) and the p-adic L-function is the n-th twist of Kubota-Leopoldt, so the conjecture becomes a twist of the Iwasawa Main Conjecture.
Remark 13.23 delimits which Tate twists are covered.
acceptance: Instantiate at V = Q_p(n) for even positive n and check the conjecture reduces to a twist of Theorem 13.8
Check that n = 0 is excluded by computing r_{Q_p^dual}
Check that the corank statement (i) is separate from the characteristic-ideal statement (ii)

sources.excerpt: (i) H^1_{L_Gr}(F,W) has Lambda(Gamma^+)-corank equal to r_V. (ii) If r_V = r_{V^dual} = 0, then the characteristic ideal of the Pontryagin dual of H^1_{L_Gr}(F,W) (as a Lambda(Gamma^+)-module) coincides with the ideal generated by the p-adic L-function of V.
sources.match: The conjecture with its two separate assertions and the explicit rank-zero hypothesis on (ii), exactly as the stage requires.

sources.excerpt: In Greenberg's terminology, L(Q_p(n),1) = zeta(1-n) and L(Q_p(n)^dual,1) = zeta(n) are both critical only when n is even and (strictly) positive, or n is odd and negative, so the case n = 0 is not covered.
sources.match: The criticality restriction the stage names as 'the even-positive/odd-negative restrictions in RJW Sec. 13.5'.

sources.excerpt: Coates-Perrin-Riou conjectured in [CPR89] that there should exist a p-adic L-function for V, which in this context lies in the field of fractions of Lambda(Gamma^+).
sources.match: Makes explicit that the existence of the p-adic L-function is an independent conjecture, so no theorem asserting existence for every motive is being introduced.

gaps.title: No determinant-line formulation for perfect Iwasawa complexes
gaps.detail: Stage L3 requires the determinant-line formulation for perfect Iwasawa complexes and its relation to characteristic ideals via PadicMeasuresIwasawaAlgebras L5. No source in the supplied library was located for determinants of perfect complexes; see the identically named gap in this job's PadicMeasuresIwasawaAlgebras packet. Nekovar's footnote (8) in the introduction remarks that 'it is natural to expect that det of H_Iw(K_infinity/K,T)' relates to p-adic L-functions, but the determinant formalism itself is not developed in the sections read. Next source action: Knudsen-Mumford, or Kato's Iwasawa-theory lectures, or Fukaya-Kato Sec. 1; none present.

gaps.title: Greenberg's original formulation and the Coates-Perrin-Riou conjecture were not read
gaps.detail: RJW Sec. 13.5.3 states Conjecture 13.21 'due to Greenberg [Gre89]' and attributes the existence of the p-adic L-function to Coates-Perrin-Riou [CPR89]. Neither paper is in the supplied library. RJW also flag that they work over Q(mu_{p^infinity})^+ whereas Greenberg works over the cyclotomic Z_p-extension, so the two formulations are not literally the same statement. VERIFIED: RJW's statement of the conjecture, its two separate assertions, the ordinarity hypothesis, the criticality restriction of Remark 13.23, and the worked instance of Example 13.22. NOT VERIFIED: Greenberg's own formulation or the precise dictionary between the two base fields. Next source action: R. Greenberg, Iwasawa theory for p-adic representations, Adv. Stud. Pure Math. 17 (1989); J. Coates and B. Perrin-Riou, On p-adic L-functions attached to motives over Q, Adv. Stud. Pure Math. 17 (1989).
